performers: Artur Schnabel, piano; London Symphony Orchestra, Malcolm Sargent
question: How does the piano change a theme the orchestra has already introduced?
intro: A quiet string march grows into an orchestral exposition before the piano offers its own account. Follow the difference between returning themes and returning keys, then hear Schnabel take responsibility for the cadenza.

sections.label: Orchestral exposition
sections.mNote: march, wind replies and orchestral cadences

sections.label: Solo exposition
sections.mNote: piano reshapes the opening and introduces further themes

sections.label: Orchestral bridge
sections.mNote: tutti closes the solo exposition and unsettles its destination

sections.label: Development
sections.mNote: new piano phrase and changing tonal centres

sections.label: Recapitulation
sections.mNote: opening march returns; later themes recover C major

sections.label: Closing ritornello
sections.mNote: orchestra recovers the cadence and ends quietly

cues.title: The orchestra speaks first
cues.text: The movement opens with a quiet march in the strings, not with the piano. Keep its short, separated notes in mind: this material will belong to several different speakers before the movement ends.
cues.evidence: The public-domain Breitkopf score, Broude reprint, p. 1, begins with strings alone. The analysis rises from a relatively quiet opening towards 0:20. This describes the opening passage, not a measured instrument entrance.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: March and sustained line
cues.text: Across the orchestral introduction, distinguish the short march figure from the longer phrases placed above it. A melody can broaden while the underlying rhythm keeps its clipped articulation.
cues.evidence: The opening score contrasts separated march notes and connected melodic writing. The report records a strong 0:20–0:40 span, then a withdrawal around 0:45; no particular orchestral part is extracted from the audio.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Withdrawal and renewed weight
cues.text: The opening does not grow in one uninterrupted crescendo. A quieter stretch gives way to another firm orchestral statement, making contrasts of weight part of the exposition before the soloist takes over.
cues.evidence: Relative level is low around 0:50–1:05, rises substantially at 1:10–1:25, then falls again. The score identifies this as part of the orchestral exposition; the measurement supports its broad contour.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: Mozart at the keyboard
cues.text: Mozart first performed K. 467 on 10 March 1785 at Vienna’s Burgtheater, in a concert given for his benefit. The concerto belongs to the period when his own playing and the supply of new works were closely connected.
cues.evidence: Hannah Chan-Hartley’s National Arts Centre programme note identifies the first performance and quotes its advertisement: https://nac-cna.ca/en/event/notes/36107
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: An entrance with a pause
cues.text: The solo exposition begins with a piano approach to a pause and trill, rather than a straightforward repetition of the orchestral opening. The strings’ march and the piano’s sustained trill can then occupy the same musical space.
cues.evidence: Score p. 6, bars 74–83, supplies the piano entrance, fermata and trill above the march. The report shows reduced brightness after 2:00 and a pronounced low-level window at 2:20; placement is approximate.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Two kinds of movement
cues.text: Through the solo exposition, separate the piano’s quick surface notes from the slower changes of harmony beneath them. Runs can extend a phrase without giving every note a new harmonic destination.
cues.evidence: The score’s solo exposition alternates melodic phrases and passagework. The report has denser detected attacks around 2:45–3:05; this is a general listening distinction, not a note-by-note alignment.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A minor-key interruption
cues.text: In this part of the solo exposition, Mozart turns towards G minor before the more settled G-major melody. The contrast lies in the altered notes and phrase shape, not in a change of movement or tempo.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 8–9 and the National Arts Centre account document the G-minor diversion before the G-major second theme. Boundaries at 3:14 and 3:24, with a darker spectral balance, support passage placement; machine key labels are not the sole evidence.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Abbey Road, January 1937
cues.text: Artur Schnabel records the concerto with the London Symphony Orchestra and Malcolm Sargent on 12 January 1937. The orchestra’s session register identifies Abbey Road Studio 1, distinguishing this event from the later LP and digital transfers.
cues.evidence: London Symphony Orchestra discography, session 0158, PDF p. 289: https://londonso-assets.s3.amazonaws.com/uploads/2024/08/Discography-August-2024.pdf#page=289
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Cadence and continuation
cues.text: Listen across this solo stretch for phrases that seem ready to settle but continue through another run or ornament. The trill is not merely decoration: it can hold the harmony in place while a cadence gathers its force.
cues.evidence: The solo exposition’s closing pages use passagework and trills before the orchestral return at bar 194. The report shows a large fall around 4:45 and renewed activity afterwards; no exact trill onset is claimed.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The solo phrase gathers
cues.text: Towards the end of the solo exposition, running figures and repeated cadential gestures accumulate. Keep listening for the change between the piano’s detailed movement and the orchestra’s more compact way of confirming a phrase.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 12–14 leads to the tutti at bar 194. The report sustains activity through 5:00–5:30, followed by a marked increase in brightness around 5:35–5:45. This is a broad approach, not a bar-aligned cue.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A bridge, not an ending
cues.text: The orchestra takes back the foreground after the solo exposition. Its cadential weight does not finish the movement: the bridge prepares a fresh piano phrase and a less settled stretch of harmony.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 14–15 places the tutti at bar 194 and the next solo at bar 222. Changes at 5:44 and 5:56, followed by quieter 6:00–6:30 windows, support the bridge’s approximate placement.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: From shellac to LP
cues.text: This stream comes from Bob Varney’s transfer of Angel COLH 67, a mono LP in the “Great Recordings of the Century” series. It is not a direct transfer of a single 1937 shellac side.
cues.evidence: The Archive description explicitly credits Bob Varney and Angel COLH 67; the cover photograph corroborates the catalogue number: https://archive.org/details/Mozart.PianoConcertoNo.21
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: A less settled centre
cues.text: The development gives the piano a fresh melodic idea before setting its passagework against changing harmonies. Listen for movement between tonal centres rather than expecting the opening exposition to repeat in order.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 15–19, beginning at bar 222, and the National Arts Centre note establish the development’s new piano theme. The report’s 6:32–6:54 changes and subsequent contrasting pitch distributions support a broad middle-section placement.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Preparing the homecoming
cues.text: Across the end of the development, rapid piano writing and sustained orchestral notes make different layers of motion. Listen for the moment when harmonic wandering gives way to the familiar march, rather than treating every run as a new theme.
cues.evidence: Score p. 19 shows running piano figures above sustained strings and winds before the opening march returns at bar 274. The report falls markedly around 7:50–7:55, then changes in brightness at 8:00.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The march comes back
cues.text: In the recapitulation, the opening march returns to C major. Recognising the tune is only part of the return: Mozart must also bring the later solo material back into the home key.
cues.evidence: Score p. 20 begins the returning march at bar 274. The 7:55–8:10 change in level and brightness supports an approximate 8:00 boundary; it does not identify a single returning note.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Not a mechanical replay
cues.text: The returning exposition changes the relationship between orchestra and soloist. Follow how familiar fragments overlap and answer one another; a recapitulation can recover the argument without restoring every detail of its first presentation.
cues.evidence: The National Arts Centre account describes overlapping entries of the march motif at the piano’s return. The report places a substantial change at 8:26; this general comparison does not time individual imitative entries.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The later theme at home
cues.text: Across the returning solo material, the theme that previously belonged to G major is brought towards C major. The important change is harmonic location: a familiar melodic contour now helps secure the movement’s home key.
cues.evidence: The score’s recapitulation transposes the later thematic area to C major. The report’s broad 9:00–9:40 span is compatible with that return; neither a precise theme onset nor an individual chord is claimed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Four discs in 1937
cues.text: HMV issued the concerto in November 1937 on four twelve-inch records, DB3099–3102. The first movement occupied four sides; the Andante and finale each occupied two. The present files join each movement into one stream.
cues.evidence: LSO discography session 0158 dates the issue; John Bolig’s HMV discography, pp. 505–506, assigns the eight sides: https://www.examenapium.it/cs/biblio/Bolig2020.pdf#page=530. No original side-join timestamps are asserted.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Increasing cadential pressure
cues.text: The later solo passage grows towards another orchestral confirmation. Follow the harmonic destination beneath the piano’s activity: the concerto still has room for an unaccompanied cadenza before its final cadence is completed.
cues.evidence: The score’s closing solo and tutti lead to the cadenza sign on p. 29. Relative level rises through 10:20–10:50 and brightness increases around 10:55–11:05; the cue concerns the broad approach.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A cadence held open
cues.text: Near the cadenza, an orchestral pause leaves the expected resolution unfinished. The piano can expand that suspended arrival into an independent solo, making a formal stopping point into space for another argument.
cues.evidence: The fermata and cadenza sign appear on score p. 29, before the concluding ritornello. Changes at 11:02 and 11:16, with reduced brightness afterwards, locate this passage approximately.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Schnabel’s own cadenza
cues.text: The first movement’s cadenza is by Schnabel. During this solo stretch, compare the freedom of the piano’s changing register and phrase lengths with the orchestra’s earlier regular march; the interruption belongs to the concerto’s design.
cues.evidence: Bolig identifies the first-movement cadenza as Schnabel’s on HMV DB3100; the score supplies the cadenza slot, not his notes. The report shows a less bright, active stretch from about 11:20 to 12:50. Its internal themes are not asserted.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Freedom before resolution
cues.text: Inside the cadenza, listen for contrasts between flowing runs and spaces where the piano lets a phrase breathe. The orchestra’s return will restore a shared pulse and complete the cadence that the solo has prolonged.
cues.evidence: The cadenza is placed between the score’s fermata and closing tutti; its detailed text is not available in the consulted full score. The report records a marked relative-level trough around 12:20 and renewed activity afterwards.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Returning to the orchestra
cues.text: Towards the end of the cadenza, the solo must lead back into the orchestra’s closing ritornello. Listen for the difference between that formal return and the earlier return of the march: this time the remaining task is to finish.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 29–30 supplies the post-cadenza ritornello. A boundary at 12:54 and the brightness increase from about 12:50 to 13:00 support its approximate placement; the cadenza’s final trill is not precisely timed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A quiet last word
cues.text: Across the closing passage, the orchestra reduces its weight rather than ending with the force of its earlier tuttis. Listen through the last C-major cadence and the remaining resonance: the quiet ending answers the quiet opening.
cues.evidence: Score p. 30 ends quietly in C major. The report falls from the renewed 13:15 activity to a much lower level at 13:25 and near silence at 13:30; no exact release time is claimed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A trill meets the march
transitions.how: The orchestral close opens into quieter wind phrases before the piano enters. Mozart then arrests the new solo line on a fermata. The piano’s trill on G overlaps the strings’ recovery of the C-major march: solo display and the old orchestral material are fitted together, rather than separated by a fresh beginning.
transitions.evidence: Score p. 6, bars 70–83. Relative level falls at 2:00, brightness remains reduced thereafter and a low-level window falls at 2:20. The 2:08 section marker represents the handover, not an exact entrance.

transitions.title: The cadence changes its speaker
transitions.how: The piano’s trill and cadential passagework give way to the orchestra at bar 194. The G-major destination reached by the solo exposition is confirmed by more compact tutti writing, but the bridge soon moves away from simple closure. Winds, brass and strings take over the argument while the piano rests.
transitions.evidence: Score pp. 13–15 supplies the trill, tutti and subsequent bridge. The report’s brightness rises sharply around 5:35–5:45; the strongest adjacent boundaries are 5:44 and 5:56. The marker is a passage estimate.

transitions.title: A new phrase opens unstable territory
transitions.how: The orchestral bridge withdraws into a new piano phrase in the minor. Mozart does not restart the march. A more lightly accompanied solo opens a development in which running figures and changing harmonies move away from the exposition’s settled tonal destinations.
transitions.evidence: Score p. 15 introduces the new solo at bar 222. The report has a pronounced quiet span at 6:20–6:30, a boundary at 6:32 and lower brightness with increased attacks from 6:35. The minor-mode character comes from the score.

transitions.title: The bass steadies beneath the march
transitions.how: The development’s moving piano line is set against increasingly sustained orchestral support. Dominant preparation makes C major available again, and the opening march returns in the strings while the soloist falls silent. The return restores a recognisable theme and tonal centre without repeating the entire opening exposition unchanged.
transitions.evidence: Score pp. 19–20, bars 264–280, shows the sustained preparation and returning march at bar 274. The report has a quiet 7:50–7:55 span and increased brightness at 8:00–8:10; this supports the broad join only.

transitions.title: The orchestra leaves a cadence unfinished
transitions.how: The closing tutti reaches a fermata over the cadential harmony. Instead of allowing the orchestra to resolve it immediately, Mozart leaves the piano alone. Schnabel’s cadenza occupies that opening: the shared orchestral pulse gives way to an extended solo before the final ritornello can complete the cadence.
transitions.evidence: Score p. 29 marks the cadenza; Bolig attributes the recorded first-movement cadenza to Schnabel. The 11:16 boundary and lower brightness around 11:20 support the approximate handover, not its precise last orchestral chord.

transitions.title: The suspended cadence finds its orchestra
transitions.how: The cadenza yields to the written orchestral ritornello, restoring a shared pulse and C-major cadential direction. The returning winds and strings provide the final confirmation, then reduce their weight towards the quiet close. The ending is not another complete exposition of the march.
transitions.evidence: Score pp. 29–30 gives the post-cadenza orchestra and quiet ending. The report’s 12:54 boundary and brighter 12:55–13:00 windows support the approximate return; later windows trace the withdrawal.

source.title: Mozart, K. 467, full score: Breitkopf & Härtel, 1878; Broude reprint, plate 422
source.locator: I, printed pp. 1–30. Passage-level scoring snapshots proportioned to the audio report; not an entrance map or identification of the performing edition. Cadenza instrumentation follows the score’s solo slot, not an engraving of Schnabel’s notes.

timeline.note: Opening passage: strings present the quiet march before the wind and brass responses.
Orchestral exposition: strings and winds exchange the material, with brass and timpani reinforcing fuller phrases.

Solo-exposition passage: piano figuration and the string march overlap. Trumpets supply held support with the winds during the entrance and fermata passage, not continuously throughout the solo exposition.
Orchestral bridge: the soloist rests while the ensemble carries the closing and linking phrases.
Early development: the new piano phrase is lightly supported by strings, with stretches of solo writing.
Development passage: moving keyboard figures are set against sustained and answering orchestral lines.
Returning orchestral passage: strings recover the march and wind replies follow; the piano initially rests.
Later recapitulation: piano material is redistributed against strings and the smaller wind group.

Pre-cadenza tutti: winds, brass, timpani and strings take over while the piano rests (score pp. 28–29, bars 384–396). The report’s brightness rise at 10:55–11:00 provisionally locates this passage, not its exact first attack.
Cadenza passage: unaccompanied piano; its detailed internal timing is not aligned.
Closing ritornello: orchestral phrases resolve the cadenza and taper towards the quiet cadence.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Artur Schnabel (piano), London Symphony Orchestra (orchestra), Malcolm Sargent (conductor)
fields.note: The Archive description, photographed LP sleeve and orchestra discography agree. Bolig and the Schnabel chronology identify a Bechstein piano. The later sleeve uses Sargent’s title Sir; that is not treated as evidence of his title at the 1937 session.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The exact performing edition is not identified. Bolig explicitly credits Artur Schnabel with the first-movement cadenza; the consulted public-domain score marks the cadenza slot but does not contain his notes. The Archive description says that an earlier file mix-up with K. 595 has been corrected; the current file attribution follows that corrected record, not the superseded review. No bar-by-bar or aural authentication of the transfer has been made.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: LSO session 0158 distinguishes K. 467, recorded on 12 January, from K. 459, recorded on 9 and 12 January. The date is independently stated in the Archive description and the side-level discographies.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: The Archive names Abbey Road Studios; the LSO register, Bolig and Schnabel chronology specify Studio 1. The recording venue is not inferred merely from the orchestra’s name.

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Angel Records — Great Recordings of the Century
fields.note: This is the documented mono LP used for Bob Varney’s transfer, not the original shellac carrier. The original recording was issued by His Master’s Voice.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The photographed sleeve prints COLH 67 and pairs K. 467 under Sargent with K. 595 under Barbirolli. LSO session 0158 dates COLH67 to November 1959 and the original K. 467 issue, HMV DB3099–3102, to November 1937. This movement originally occupied DB3099 and DB3100.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: Probable original-side lineage: 2EA 4604-1, 2EA 4605-1, 2EA 4606-1 and 2EA 4607-2A; first movement parts 1–4 on HMV DB3099–3100.
fields.note: Those issued matrix/take numbers are explicitly documented by Bolig and the Schnabel chronology. Their survival in this particular Angel LP transfer is inferred, not established by runout inspection or take comparison. The LP’s own matrix/runout and pressing are unknown. No original side-join timestamps are assigned. A targeted DAHR search produced no directly usable session record, so no DAHR matrix entry is claimed.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: The source expressly states ‘Transfer by Bob Varney’; this credit is not inferred from the uploader account.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The item was added on 19 April 2010, and the current MP3 has a later file timestamp following the documented correction. Neither is an identified analogue-to-digital transfer date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: The source identifies a mono LP transfer but gives no cartridge, equalisation, noise-reduction, editing or speed-correction procedure. Internet Archive labels the uploaded file VBR MP3 and original; ‘original’ here means the uploaded file, not an original session master.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Mozart’s concerto is public domain under the ordinary life-plus-70 term; Schnabel’s own cadenza is also beyond that term.
fields.note: Mozart died in 1791; the consulted score derives from the 1878 Breitkopf edition. Schnabel died in 1951, giving an ordinary life-plus-70 expiry at the end of 2021 for his authorship. This is a territorial term calculation, not clearance of every modern edition or a claim about US cadenza publication history.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: territorial — EU public-domain basis: first published in November 1937 on HMV DB3099–3102.
fields.note: The LSO discography documents publication before 1963, independently of the 1937 session date. The ordinary EU 50-year sound-recording term had expired before the 2013 extension, which applies to recordings still protected at that date. This package uses that territorial basis only. US public-domain status is not established: this is not a recording first published by 1925. The Archive uploader links http://creativecommons.org/licenses/publicdomain/, but that declaration does not independently establish authority to release the performers’ or producer’s rights worldwide. The linked legal URL below is the term basis, not a Creative Commons grant.

composer.epithet: An opera composer whose instrumental music gives different voices the freedom to disagree.
facts: By his father Leopold; extensive performing tours from childhood
Salzburg · Italy · Mannheim and Paris · Vienna from 1781
Italian opera seria and opera buffa; German Singspiel with spoken dialogue
K. or KV = Ludwig von Köchel’s catalogue, first published in 1862 and repeatedly revised
composer.background:
Mozart was born in Salzburg in 1756, the seventh child of Leopold Mozart and Anna Maria Pertl; only he and his sister Maria Anna survived infancy. Leopold was a violinist and composer in the archbishop’s service, and in the year of Wolfgang’s birth published an influential violin treatise. He taught both children. Maria Anna, called Nannerl within the family, became an accomplished keyboard player, and the first tours presented brother and sister together. The family’s travels were an educational system as well as a business: the children encountered instruments, performers, repertories and audiences that a Salzburg childhood alone could not have supplied.

The long tour of 1763–66 took them through German courts, Paris, London and the Netherlands. In London Mozart met Johann Christian Bach, whose clear phrases and Italianate melodic style offered a model different from the contrapuntal teaching associated with Bach’s father. Illness repeatedly interrupted the itinerary. Leopold managed engagements, publicity and money while supervising composition, and the surviving correspondence documents the costs and uncertainties behind the public demonstrations. Wolfgang learned to write for named performers and immediate occasions before he had an independent adult household.
